finding.claim: Unauthenticated GET /mirror passes a user-supplied url to httpx after a bare suffix check, so an attacker can make the server fetch any host whose name ends in 'example.com', e.g. evilexample.com, which the attacker's DNS can point at internal addresses.
finding.source: mirror.py:11 - query parameter 'url' on the unauthenticated GET /mirror route

trace.note: url: str taken from query string; no auth dependency on the route
host.endswith('example.com') - suffix match without dot boundary; evilexample.com passes
same unmodified url string passed to httpx GET

finding.guards_checked: Host check result is used (400 at line 14) and blocks evil.com, example.com.evil.com, and userinfo/fragment/query tricks; urllib and httpx parse those identically (httpx/_urlparse.py:125-134, 289-313). Redirects are not followed (httpx default follow_redirects=False, httpx/_client.py:197). Only http/https schemes reach the wire. Missing: dot-boundary check; ALLOWED_SUFFIX at line 7 is unused; no resolved-IP / private-range / loopback / link-local block; no port restriction. Impact is limited to a response length oracle and status-code oracle, but the outbound request to internal targets is still made.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only check is mirror.py:13 `host.endswith("example.com")`, a suffix match with no dot boundary, so `evilexample.com` passes. Nothing else on the path validates the host: no resolved-IP or private-range block, no port restriction, and ALLOWED_SUFFIX (line 7) is unused.
verdict.reason: The `url` query parameter on the unauthenticated `/mirror` route (mirror.py:11) reaches `httpx.AsyncClient().get(url)` at mirror.py:16 after the suffix-only check at mirror.py:13, which accepts an attacker-owned host like `evilexample.com` that can resolve to internal addresses. The trace matches the code, and the impact is a blind SSRF (the server makes the request, and only `len(r.text)` at line 17 is returned).
